posts.text:
Sitting in court watching Stephen Gray’s appeal against a conviction for reposting a meme which mocked Islam and Muhammad marrying a child. He had 15-20 followers on Facebook. A (non-Muslim!) neighbour, who Stephen has previous disagreements with, decided to report him to the police claiming it caused him distress… 

The fundamental argument from the CPS is that Stephen was not making a political point. That he expressed his objection to Islamic child marriage in a way that was simply to offend because it singled out Islam, and he should have made his post more nuanced and sensitive if he was making a political point. 

The defence is having to point out that Muhammad did in fact marry a 6 year old according to Islamic texts, and that child marriage does still occur in Islamic countries AND there are prominent Islamic scholars IN THE UK who openly say that they are content with child marriage. And either way, it is not illegal to offend others, and you are allowed to make political points that are not nuanced. 

To think of all the actual, serious crime in Middlesbrough — let alone the rest of the country — and the time being wasted on this nonsense. Actually witnessing the amount of public resource and time being funnelled into prosecuting people for causing offence by highlighting a factual point is acutely infuriating. 

Anyway, join the @SpeechUnion because you never know when it might be you having to explain why you don’t like child marriage, or anything else that Islam permits.

posts.text:
Zambia has started connecting 751 health facilities across all 10 provinces with Starlink, and the first 90 kits went to Western Province.

There's something poetic about where they started. Every year at the end of the rainy season the upper Zambezi floods the Barotse plain, and for centuries the Lozi king has left his compound at Lealui by royal barge and moved to higher ground at Limulunga. The ceremony is called Kuomboka. In Lozi it means "to get out of water."

Now picture running fiber or building towers across land that turns into a lake for part of every year. A Starlink dish only needs a clear view of the sky, so the water below stops being the problem.

In March 2020, months before Starlink had its first beta users, Elon Musk said it would serve the 3 or 4 percent hardest-to-reach customers, people with no connectivity or really bad connectivity. Six years later, with funding from the Global Fund through Zambia's Ministry of Health, clinics on one of Africa's great floodplains are being brought into the country's electronic health systems from orbit.

posts.text:
Brock Lesnar promised he was still the baddest man on the planet. Two minutes and twenty-six seconds later, a body kick from Alistair Overeem ended his UFC career forever.

On December 30, 2011, at UFC 141 in Las Vegas, Lesnar stepped into the cage for the first time in over a year. Months earlier he had undergone major surgery that removed 12 inches of his colon after a second bout with diverticulitis forced him out of a fight against Junior dos Santos. 

He had called the Overeem bout his chance to prove the disease was behind him. Overeem, the heavy-handed K-1 and Strikeforce champion making his UFC debut, had other ideas. He said Lesnar’s weaknesses were his strengths and guaranteed a finish inside two rounds.

Overeem delivered. Knees and kicks to the body dropped Lesnar; punches on the ground finished it. In the post-fight interview Lesnar, still processing the loss, tipped his hat to Overeem and announced his retirement on the spot, citing the “difficult couple of years” with his illness. 

The pre-fight hype had framed it as a clash of giants. The reality was a one-sided dismantling that closed the book on Lesnar’s MMA run.
